passage: In the courtyard of their apartment block in Addis Ababa, Abebe got angry when Mina's kite flew higher than his. He grabbed her string and yanked, and the kite tore on the railing. Mina burst into tears and ran inside. Abebe stood alone with his own kite, feeling sick. He didn't want to fly it anymore. After ten minutes he knocked on Mina's door. "I'm sorry I pulled it. I was jealous." Mina sniffed. "It's ripped." "My grandmother has tape and paper. Can I help fix it?" They sat on the stairs with his grandmother's tape, patching the torn corner with an old calendar page. It looked funny, but it held. By evening both kites were up again. Abebe laughed out loud when Mina's patched one wobbled past his, and the sick feeling was gone.

qa.q: What did Abebe and Mina use to patch the kite?
qa.a: They used his grandmother's tape and an old calendar page.

qa.q: How did Abebe feel standing alone after the kite tore?
qa.a: He felt sick and guilty, so bad that he didn't want to fly his own kite anymore.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Apologising honestly and helping repair the kite worked, because it fixed the harm and let both children play together again.

qa.q: How might Mina have felt when Abebe offered to help?
qa.a: Mina was probably still hurt, but comforted that he admitted his jealousy and wanted to make it right.

grounding: Shows a child who hurt a friend apologising and helping repair the damage, after which he can play again and the guilt eases.

passage: During the Class 4 art period at Greenfield School, Chaitanya bumped Elizabeth's water jar on purpose because she had laughed at his drawing. Grey water ran all over her painted lighthouse. Elizabeth stared at it, then put her head down on the desk. Chaitanya felt his face burn. He spent the next five minutes pretending to sharpen a pencil. Then he went over. "I did that on purpose. I'm sorry. I was cross because you laughed." Elizabeth lifted her head. "It's ruined." "Can I help you paint a new one? I'm good at waves." Their teacher gave them a fresh sheet. Chaitanya did the waves, Elizabeth did the lighthouse. At break, they played tag together as if nothing had happened, and Chaitanya ran faster than he had all week.

qa.q: What had Elizabeth painted?
qa.a: A lighthouse.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling while he pretended to sharpen a pencil?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and guilty, his face burning, unsure how to face Elizabeth.

qa.q: Why did helping paint the new picture matter more than just saying sorry?
qa.a: It actually repaired the damage and let them do something together, so both could move past it and play at break.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt when Chaitanya admitted it was on purpose?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a little relieved that he told the truth, which made it easier to trust his offer of help.

grounding: Shows a child who spoiled a classmate's work apologising and helping repair it, then being able to play freely again.

passage: I'm Zubin's neighbour on the fourth floor, and I saw the whole thing from our balcony. Zubin and Manjula were building a fort from old cartons on the terrace. They argued about the door, and Zubin kicked the whole side in. Manjula shouted and sat down with her back to him. Zubin stood there for a long time, kicking at nothing. I don't know what he was thinking. Then he went downstairs and came back with more cartons and a roll of tape from his mother. He said something to Manjula that I couldn't hear. She shrugged. He started rebuilding the side by himself. After a while, she began holding the cartons for him. By sunset the fort had a new door, a bigger one. I heard them both laughing inside it.

qa.q: Where were Zubin and Manjula building the fort?
qa.a: On the terrace, from old cartons.

qa.q: What does Zubin standing there kicking at nothing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt upset and uneasy, perhaps guilty, though the neighbour can't be sure what he was thinking.

qa.q: What small step did Zubin take to repair things?
qa.a: He fetched more cartons and tape, said something to Manjula, and started rebuilding the side he broke by himself.

qa.q: How did Manjula's feelings seem to change?
qa.a: She went from shouting and turning her back to holding the cartons and laughing inside the fort, which suggests she felt ready to forgive.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a child repair the fort he broke, after which both children could play again.

passage:
"Chinmay, you look like you're chewing on something," said Hansa Ba, tapping the swing beside her. "Sit. Let me tell you about the school annual day when I was sixteen. I had one line in the play. One line! And I said it wrong: instead of 'The king is coming,' I said 'The cow is coming.' The hall laughed for a full minute.
For three weeks I replayed it every night. I stopped going near the auditorium. I told myself I deserved every laugh, that I was punishing myself for being careless. I even skipped my friend Kokila's dance recital so I wouldn't have to be in that hall.
Then Kokila came home with me one evening, crying because I'd missed it. I saw my 'punishment' was only hurting people. Next year, I auditioned again. And I still say 'the cow is coming' when your Dada is late for dinner."

qa.q: What did Hansa Ba say instead of 'The king is coming'?
qa.a: She said 'The cow is coming.'

qa.q: What did Hansa Ba feel during those three weeks of replaying it?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and kept blaming herself, believing she deserved every laugh.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Hansa Ba stop punishing herself?
qa.a: Kokila coming home crying about the missed recital, which showed that the self-punishment was only hurting people; after that she auditioned again.

qa.q: How was Kokila affected by Hansa's avoidance?
qa.a: Kokila was hurt and upset, crying because her friend missed her dance recital.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how replaying an embarrassing slip at sixteen felt like accountability but led only to shame and avoidance.

passage: It was exam week, the geography project was due Friday, and Bhupen couldn't stop hearing his own voice. On Monday, in front of the whole group, he'd snapped at Trisha: "Can you do anything right?" She'd gone quiet and finished her map without looking up. Since then Bhupen had replayed it maybe a hundred times: on the bus, in the shower, at 2 am. He told himself he was a terrible person. He thought he was taking responsibility. But he stopped going to the group's library meetings. He sent his part by email so he wouldn't have to see Trisha. On Thursday, the project still missing her section on rivers, he forced himself to text: "Trisha, I was awful on Monday. I'm sorry. Can we finish the river part together?" She replied in five minutes: "ok. library at 4?"

qa.q: What did Bhupen snap at Trisha?
qa.a: He snapped, 'Can you do anything right?'

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling during the days he replayed the remark?
qa.a: Bhupen felt ashamed and guilty, calling himself a terrible person, and anxious enough to avoid seeing Trisha.

qa.q: What would you advise Bhupen the next time he catches himself replaying a mistake?
qa.a: Turn the replay into one action, such as a quick honest apology, instead of punishing himself and hiding.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt during the days Bhupen avoided the group?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and confused, still stung by the remark and left to finish the project without him.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying a harsh remark for days, feeling it as accountability while it mostly produces shame and avoidance.

passage: At the Monday assembly in her Dehradun school, Charu's voice cracked on the word "gratitude" during the thought for the day. It came out as a squeak. A few juniors giggled. The rest of the day was normal for everyone else. For Charu, it wasn't. At lunch she heard the squeak in her head. At home she lay on her bed and replayed it again and again, each time adding worse details. "Everyone thinks I'm a joke," she told her friend Lavanya on the phone that night. By Wednesday she had asked the teacher to take her off the assembly list. Lavanya came over with a bag of chikki. "Charu, I was standing right there. I barely noticed. You've heard it fifty times. We heard it once." Charu laughed despite herself. She wasn't sure yet. But she didn't cancel the Friday slot after all.

qa.q: Which word did Charu's voice crack on?
qa.a: Gratitude.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling as she replayed the squeak at home?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and ashamed, adding worse details each time and believing everyone thought she was a joke.

qa.q: How did Lavanya help Charu see the slip differently?
qa.a: She reminded Charu that she had heard it fifty times while others heard it once, which shrank the moment back to its real size.

qa.q: What would change if Charu had kept avoiding the assembly?
qa.a: The shame would probably have grown and she would have missed the chance to speak again and prove the squeak didn't define her.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying an embarrassing moment for days, which produces shame and avoidance rather than growth.

passage: Felix had shared a flat in Leipzig with Clara for a year, and he'd started counting. The broken kettle: "Not my fault, it was old." The rent paid late: "Not my fault, the bank was slow." Last night she'd forgotten to lock the front door and his bike was stolen. "It's not my fault, the lock is stiff." Felix believed some of these. But he noticed that Clara never seemed lighter after saying it. She'd been snappy all morning and kept checking the empty spot where the bike had been. At lunch he said, carefully, "I'm not trying to blame you. It's just a bike." Clara put her fork down. After a long pause she said, "I forgot the door. I'm really sorry." Her voice cracked. She looked, for the first time in weeks, relieved.

qa.q: What was stolen after Clara forgot to lock the door?
qa.a: Felix's bike.

qa.q: How did Felix feel, noticing that Clara never seemed lighter after her excuses?
qa.a: Felix felt puzzled and a little concerned, sensing that the excuses were not easing her guilt.

qa.q: What did Felix say that made it easier for Clara to own the mistake?
qa.a: He said calmly that he wasn't trying to blame her and it was just a bike, which lowered the stakes enough for her to admit it.

qa.q: What was it like for Clara to finally say 'I forgot the door'?
qa.a: It was hard, since her voice cracked, but she looked relieved for the first time in weeks.

grounding: Shows a flatmate noticing that someone's repeated 'not my fault' leaves guilt unresolved, and that owning the harm brings relief.

passage: At the biotech lab on the third floor, Avni watched Amandeep open the freezer and go pale. The samples for their project, six weeks of work, had thawed. Amandeep had left the door ajar the night before. "It's not my fault," Amandeep said immediately. "This freezer is ancient. Someone should have fixed the seal." Avni nodded, but she'd seen the door open at seven. For the next two days Amandeep snapped at everyone, skipped the team lunch, and kept muttering about the seal. Avni wasn't sure what to say. On Thursday, while they were restarting the cultures, Amandeep stopped pipetting. "I left it open. I checked my phone and walked off." Avni just said, "Okay. Thanks for saying it." Amandeep let out a long breath. The rest of the afternoon, the snapping stopped.

qa.q: How many weeks of work had thawed in the freezer?
qa.a: Six weeks of work.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when Amandeep blamed the freezer?
qa.a: Avni felt uneasy and unsure what to say, since she had seen the door open at seven.

qa.q: Why did Avni's simple reply help?
qa.a: She didn't scold or lecture; she thanked Amandeep for owning it, which let the guilt finally ease.

qa.q: How was Amandeep affected by admitting the mistake?
qa.a: Amandeep let out a long breath and stopped snapping, which suggests the unresolved guilt had been weighing heavily.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing that repeated excuses leave someone's guilt unresolved, and that owning the harm lets them move on.

passage:
Dear Minakshi,

I've wanted to write this for a while, and it's easier on paper.

When you missed my birthday dinner, you said the auto driver got lost. When you forgot to return my exam notes before the test, you said your mother had moved them. When you told Sneha what I'd shared in confidence, you said, "It's not my fault, she asked me directly."

Maybe some of those are true. But I've noticed you look more stressed every time you say it, not less. It's like the excuse stops the conversation before anything can be put right.

I'm not angry anymore. I just miss how we used to be. If you ever want to say "I messed up," I'll be here to hear it, and I'll forgive you faster than you think.

Mehak

qa.q: What did Minakshi say about telling Sneha what Mehak shared?
qa.a: Minakshi said, 'It's not my fault, she asked me directly.'

qa.q: How does Mehak seem to feel about the excuses?
qa.a: Mehak seems sad and missing the old friendship, no longer angry but worried that the excuses keep Minakshi stressed.

qa.q: What small step does Mehak invite Minakshi to take?
qa.a: To simply say 'I messed up', which would let them repair things and let Minakshi forgive herself.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Minakshi might feel exposed and defensive at first, but perhaps relieved that Mehak is ready to forgive.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that someone's repeated excuses skip owning the harm and leave the guilt unresolved.

passage:
March: Akash sat in his room in Indore, surrounded by the engineering books he'd stopped opening a year ago. He'd spent that year gaming at night and sleeping till noon, then dropped out. Now he wouldn't apply anywhere. "Why should I get a second chance after wasting one?" he told his friend Tarun.
A week later: Tarun came over and asked, "What did you know then that you know now?" Akash was quiet a long time. "That I hated the course. That I didn't know how to say it." Tarun said, "So you were a nineteen-year-old doing the best you knew."
May: Akash filled in the form for a design diploma. His hands shook when he clicked submit. He still felt the old sting about that year, but he let himself apply anyway.

qa.q: How did Akash spend the year before he dropped out?
qa.a: He spent that year gaming at night and sleeping till noon.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling in March when he refused to apply?
qa.a: He felt guilty and ashamed, believing he didn't deserve a second chance after wasting one.

qa.q: What small step helped Akash begin to forgive himself?
qa.a: Tarun's question about what he knew then, which helped Akash see his younger self as doing the best he knew rather than as someone to punish.

qa.q: How might Tarun have seen Akash's refusal to apply?
qa.a: Tarun probably saw it as punishment that kept Akash stuck, and cared enough to come over and gently question it.

grounding: Shows a young adult who punished himself for a wasted year learning that his past self did the best it knew, allowing him to move forward.

passage:
"Varun, I see you sitting with that rejection letter like it's a sentence from a judge," said Parul bua, settling on the sofa. "Let me tell you about me at twenty. I was with a boy in college and I was careless with him. I cancelled on him, I mocked his poems in front of friends. He ended it, and he was right to.
For two years after that I punished myself. I wouldn't let anyone close. I turned down the theatre group I loved because he'd been in it. I thought refusing good things was the least I deserved.
Then my Nani said something I've kept ever since: 'At twenty you did what you knew at twenty. Now you know more. Use it.' I wrote to him and apologised properly. Then I joined the theatre group. I was kinder in my next relationship because of him."

qa.q: What did Parul bua mock in front of friends?
qa.a: She mocked his poems in front of friends.

qa.q: What was Parul bua feeling during the two years after the breakup?
qa.a: She felt guilty and undeserving, refusing good things as a kind of punishment.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Parul bua move forward?
qa.a: Her Nani's words that at twenty she did what she knew at twenty; after that she apologised properly and joined the theatre group.

qa.q: How might the boy from college have felt on receiving her apology?

passage: The audition hall had no power, the rain was hammering the tin roof, and the director was holding auditions by phone torch. Jahnavi stood outside the door, soaked, not going in. Two years ago, the night before the college play, she had panicked and walked out, leaving her team without a lead. She hadn't auditioned for anything since. "You don't get to be in plays after doing that," she told Avni, who had dragged her there. Avni pulled her under the awning. "What did you know then?" Jahnavi thought. "That I was scared. That I didn't know how to tell anyone." "So you were eighteen and panicking, and you did what you knew. You've already apologised to everyone." Jahnavi breathed. The rain didn't stop. She went in anyway, and did her monologue by torchlight.

qa.q: How was the director holding auditions?
qa.a: By phone torch, since the hall had no power.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling outside the audition door?
qa.a: She felt guilty and unworthy, believing that after walking out two years ago she didn't deserve to be in plays.

qa.q: How did Avni help Jahnavi move forward?
qa.a: Avni asked what Jahnavi knew then and reminded her she'd already apologised, helping her see her past self as scared, not bad.

qa.q: What would change if Jahnavi had kept punishing herself?
qa.a: She would keep losing chances she loves, like acting, without making anything better for her old team.

grounding: Shows a young adult who punished herself for a past failure learning that her younger self did what it knew, and moving forward.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Missed the quarterly report deadline today. My manager had to explain it to the client, and she looked tired, not angry, which was worse.
On the bus home I heard the old voice: "You're hopeless. You always do this." Then I tried the thing the counsellor suggested. If Jaya had missed this deadline, what would I tell her?
I'd say: "You made an error. You took on the vendor audit and the report in the same week, and you didn't flag it early. That's the mistake. But you also stayed late every day and checked every number twice. That counts."
So I wrote it down, to me. It felt silly. Then it helped. Tomorrow I'll tell my manager I should have flagged the clash on Friday, and I'll suggest a check-in rule for weeks like this.
Pradeep

qa.q: What deadline did Pradeep miss?
qa.a: The quarterly report deadline.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: Pradeep felt ashamed and self-critical at first, hearing the voice call him hopeless, before trying a kinder approach.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's kinder note do better than 'You're hopeless'?
qa.a: It names the real error and the effort, which leads to a clear fix like flagging clashes early instead of just self-blame.

qa.q: How might the manager see Pradeep's plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: The manager would probably feel reassured and respect Pradeep more for owning the error and suggesting a fix.

grounding: Shows a person speaking to themselves after a failure as they would to a friend, naming the error and the effort, which leads to better change.

passage: Lokesh walked home along the canal path from the village school in Sirsa, dust on his shoes and a knot in his stomach. The district inspector had watched his science lesson that morning, and it had gone badly. The seed experiment didn't sprout, two boys fought, and he lost track of time. "Idiot," he muttered at the sugarcane. Then he stopped. His sister Lakshmi had failed her first lesson inspection last year, and he'd sat with her on the roof and said all the right things. He tried saying them to himself, out loud, feeling a bit foolish. "Okay. The seeds were planted too late. That's the error. The fight, you handled calmly. You're three months into the job and you care about these kids." By the time he reached the gate, the knot had loosened. He wrote "plant seeds a week earlier" in his notebook.

qa.q: What went wrong with the seed experiment?
qa.a: The seeds didn't sprout because they were planted too late.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling on the walk home at first?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and tense, with a knot in his stomach, calling himself an idiot.

qa.q: What did talking to himself as he talked to Lakshmi make possible?
qa.a: It helped him name the real error and his effort, so he left with a practical fix: plant seeds a week earlier.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi react if she heard what he told himself?
qa.a: She would probably feel touched and proud that the words he once gave her were now helping him.

grounding: Shows a young teacher speaking to himself after a failed lesson as he would to his sister, naming the error and the effort.

passage: In their Lajpat Nagar flat, Zubin, five, packed his little bag for tomorrow's picnic: one ball, two biscuits, his toy giraffe. "It will be sunny," he told Dolma from next door. "I promised a picnic, and we'll have one." He spread the mat on the balcony. They ate biscuits and watched the rain. Zubin giggled. "Tomorrow's picnic can be sunny."

passage:
Before the spelling bee in Class 5, I practised every night with a notebook Amma gave me. I wrote the hard words on one side and made up tricks on the other. "Rhythm has your two hips moving," that kind of thing. I kept thinking: if I get through ten words each night, I can reach the final.
Chaitanya, my desk partner, said he'd just "pray and see." He kept a lucky rubber in his pocket.
The more I practised, the more I hoped, and the more I hoped, the more I wanted to practise. It was like a wheel.
On the day, I got to the final round and went out on "conscientious." I was sad, but also proud. Chaitanya went out on the second word and looked really surprised.
I'm Disha, and I still keep that notebook.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya keep in his pocket?
qa.a: A lucky rubber.

qa.q: How did Disha feel after going out in the final round?
qa.a: Disha felt sad but also proud, knowing the practice had made it to the final.

qa.q: What would you advise Chaitanya before the next spelling bee?
qa.a: Keep the lucky rubber if it helps, but add a small nightly practice plan, like ten words a night, so the hope has a path.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya have been surprised to go out so early?

grounding: Shows a child whose hope for a spelling bee is tied to steady practice, keeping effort alive, compared with a friend who only wishes.

passage: In a Chicago high school, Bilal got his chemistry exam back with a big red D. He'd studied for two weeks. On the bus he stared out of the window. passage: In the school counsellor's room in Ludhiana, Baljeet sat with his arms folded, the physics marks list crumpled in his fist. "I failed. Again. There's no use trying. He talked, fast and angry, for ten minutes. She listened. Then she asked, "Of the six chapters, is there one that felt a little less bad?" Baljeet thought. "Optics. Maybe." "Mrs. Gill runs a lunchtime group for optics on Tuesdays. I can walk you there now to sign up." Baljeet looked at the door. Then at her. "Now?" "Now." He unclenched his fist, smoothed the marks list, and stood up. She called his father that afternoon to share the plan.

Last autumn, Lalremsiami tore a ligament two weeks before the state football trials. She had trained for three years. When I found her in the physio room at school, she wasn't crying. She was just staring at the wall, which was worse.
I wanted to say, "You'll be back stronger," because everyone was saying that. I could see it made her flinch.
So I just sat down. I stayed there through the whole of the next period, which got me a warning. She talked a little about her dad, who'd driven her to every practice. Then she was quiet.
Before I left I asked, "Can I bring my laptop tomorrow? We can watch the trials together, and you can tell me who you'd pick." She almost smiled. "Okay."
I'm Amandeep. We watched every match. She tried out again the next year.

"Nandini, you're sulking at that rejection email as if it's the last ship leaving," said Thomas uncle, laughing. "Let me tell you about 1989. I was twenty-one, trying to get on a merchant ship as a cadet. I went to the shipping offices in Kochi every Monday for eight months. Every Monday, no. Some clerks knew me by name. One gave me tea out of pity.
My friend Jacob said, 'If it's meant to be, it'll come.' He stopped going. He waited for a letter that never came.
I didn't know if I'd ever get a berth. I knew only that if I stopped going, I definitely wouldn't. On the thirty-fourth Monday, a captain needed someone that day. I was standing there.
It wasn't fate, kutty. It was being there on the day, without knowing."
